Family Health

Can pregnancy happen after endometrial ablation?

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Yes. Endometrial ablation can reduce heavy periods, but it is not contraception. A later pregnancy can be dangerous, so future pregnancy wishes and an effective contraceptive plan must be discussed before treatment.

The aim is to reduce heavy menstrual bleeding

Endometrial ablation treats the lining inside the uterus, called the endometrium, so that less tissue bleeds during periods. It may make bleeding lighter or stop it, but it does not remove the uterus. It is different from a hysterectomy and from surgery to treat endometriosis outside the uterine cavity.

A clinician may discuss it when heavy periods have not improved enough with medicines or other suitable options. Frequently soaking through pads or tampons, prolonged bleeding, anaemia and disruption to everyday life all deserve assessment. A single two-hour product-change rule does not decide who needs an operation. The cause of bleeding, the shape of the uterus and your future pregnancy wishes must be considered first.

Pregnancy is still possible and can be dangerous

Ablation is not sterilisation and must not be relied on as contraception. The ovaries may continue releasing eggs, and enough lining may remain for a pregnancy to begin. Lighter periods, or no periods, do not prove that pregnancy is impossible.

The damaged or scarred lining makes a pregnancy after ablation high risk. Miscarriage, pregnancy outside the usual uterine location and abnormal placental attachment are important concerns, with potentially serious bleeding. A pregnancy can occur without being safe to continue in the usual way. If you want to carry a pregnancy in future, ablation is not an appropriate choice; discuss a different approach before proceeding.

Lining can remain or regrow

Ablation does not always destroy every part of the lining permanently. Pockets of functioning tissue may remain or grow again over months or years. This helps explain why bleeding can return, sometimes with cyclical pain when scar tissue obstructs the normal passage of blood.

Later symptoms are sometimes described as late-onset ablation failure. They need assessment rather than an assumption that the whole uterus has returned to its earlier state. Regrowth does not restore the safety of carrying a pregnancy. Younger people may face a longer period during which recurrent symptoms can develop, so the expected durability of treatment is part of the initial discussion.

Discuss alternatives before making an irreversible decision

If pregnancy plans are uncertain, say so before agreeing to treatment. Depending on the cause of bleeding, options may include medicines that reduce menstrual blood loss, hormonal treatment, a suitable hormonal intrauterine system or treatment directed at a particular fibroid or polyp. Each option has its own benefits, restrictions and effect on fertility.

You should have time to consider symptom relief alongside future family plans. An ablation is not a temporary fertility pause that can reliably be reversed later. If a major treatment decision feels overwhelming, ask for another discussion or referral. A counsellor or therapist can help with the emotional side without deciding for you which outcome matters most.

Ovarian-reserve tests do not measure egg quality directly

A fertility specialist may use anti-Müllerian hormone, or AMH, follicle-stimulating hormone, or FSH, and ultrasound findings to help assess ovarian reserve. These tests provide information about the remaining egg supply and potential response to stimulation; they do not directly prove that eggs are good quality.

A reassuring result cannot guarantee pregnancy, a healthy embryo or a live birth. Age and other reproductive factors matter too. If preserving eggs or embryos is being considered, discuss it before ablation. Testing the ovaries also does not test whether a scarred uterine lining can safely support a pregnancy.

Freezing eggs or embryos does not make the uterus safe for pregnancy

Egg or embryo freezing can preserve a possibility of future fertility treatment, but some eggs do not survive thawing or develop into embryos, and not every embryo results in a baby. It cannot reverse the effects of ablation on the uterus. Do not choose the procedure on the assumption that stored eggs guarantee a later pregnancy you can carry yourself.

Depending on circumstances, a specialist may discuss a gestational carrier using an embryo created with your own or donor eggs. Donor treatment and surrogacy involve medical, emotional, practical and legal considerations, with availability varying by location. Adoption may be another route to parenthood, with its own process rather than a guaranteed substitute. These are possibilities to explore if relevant, not steps everyone undergoing ablation must take.

Agree on contraception before treatment

Use a reliable contraceptive plan before the procedure and continue it afterwards until menopause, unless pregnancy is already prevented by an appropriate permanent method. Discuss which option suits your health and preferences with the clinician. Permanent contraception may be considered, but ablation itself is not a permanent contraceptive procedure.

Do not use the absence of periods after ablation to decide that contraception is no longer needed. Ask how menopause and the stopping point for your method will be assessed. Condoms also help reduce sexually transmitted infection risk; ablation and other contraceptive methods do not provide that protection. A plan for infection prevention and a plan to avoid pregnancy may therefore involve more than one measure.

Checks before ablation

The team reviews your medical and surgical history, medicines, allergies and current symptoms. Pregnancy must be excluded, and an intrauterine device must be removed before ablation. The uterine lining is sampled to check for cancer or precancerous changes, with imaging or hysteroscopy used when needed to assess the cavity.

Current infection, concerning tissue results, an unsuitable cavity or certain previous uterine operations may change whether a particular method can be used. Ablation is generally for premenopausal people whose childbearing is complete. It is not a treatment to bypass investigation of unexplained bleeding or suspected cancer. Ask what the results show and why the proposed device is suitable.

Preparation and anaesthesia vary

Some techniques work best after the lining has been thinned with medication or a dilation and curettage procedure, known as D&C. This is not required in the same way for every device. The cervix may also need preparation or gentle dilation so the instruments can pass into the uterus.

An office procedure may use local anaesthesia and pain relief, while another technique may use regional or general anaesthesia. Follow the specific instructions about eating, drinking and medicines; do not apply an eight-hour fast to every appointment. Further tests, such as an ECG, are selected according to your health and anaesthetic assessment rather than automatically needed for everyone. Arrange transport and support as instructed.

1. Freezing the lining

Cryoablation uses extreme cold to damage the lining. Systems differ: some use a cooled probe, while others use a balloon-based device. Ultrasound may guide or monitor treatment. The uterine cavity and the particular system determine the application pattern and duration. A short description of one device should not be taken as instructions for all freezing methods.

2. A heated balloon

With balloon ablation, a balloon is positioned within the uterus and filled with fluid that is heated. Heat transferred through the balloon treats the lining. Cavity dimensions and device limits matter, and the clinician checks that the system can be used safely in your uterus. The treatment and total appointment time are different; a few minutes of energy delivery does not describe the whole visit.

3. Heated fluid flowing through the cavity

Hydrothermal ablation circulates heated fluid, usually saline, within the uterine cavity under controlled conditions. It can sometimes be considered when the cavity is irregular, but that does not make every abnormal uterine shape suitable. The team must check the anatomy, control the fluid and follow the device’s safety limits. The method is chosen for clinical suitability, not simply personal preference.

4. Radiofrequency treatment

A radiofrequency system places a device within the cavity, often expanding a flexible mesh to contact the lining. Energy is applied to destroy the target tissue, and the device is then removed. In some systems the energy application lasts only a minute or two, but assessment, anaesthesia and recovery add to the visit. Ask which system is planned and what limitations apply.

5. Microwave treatment

Microwave ablation applies energy through a probe to treat the endometrium. It is another technique described in ablation guidance, but availability and the particular devices in use vary between health systems and over time. A quoted three-to-five-minute treatment period is not a universal promise. The clinician should explain the locally available method rather than implying all listed technologies are offered everywhere.

6. Electrosurgical treatment

An electrosurgical approach uses a viewing scope and an instrument such as a wire loop, rollerball or electrode to remove or destroy lining. This may be called endometrial resection or electrocautery ablation, depending on the technique. It is performed with an appropriate anaesthetic, often in an operating setting. The anaesthetic plan and fluid monitoring differ from a simple office appointment.

What early recovery can feel like

Period-like cramps, nausea and light bleeding may occur soon after treatment. A watery discharge mixed with blood can continue for several weeks. Some people need to urinate more often briefly. Ask which symptoms and duration are expected for your procedure, which pain or nausea medicine is appropriate and what should trigger a call.

Use pads as directed and follow the instructions about tampons, cups, bathing, swimming and penetrative sex. Local aftercare intervals differ; your team’s written advice should take priority over a generic timetable. After sedation or general anaesthesia, arrange collection and supervision and follow restrictions on driving and caring for others. Feeling well enough to leave the unit does not mean those restrictions have ended.

Possible complications include injury and later symptoms

Uncommon serious complications include significant bleeding, infection, a tear in the uterus, and injury to nearby structures such as the bowel or bladder. Heat or cold can damage tissue beyond the intended lining. Some techniques also carry risks related to fluid entering the bloodstream. Risks depend on the method and individual circumstances.

Later problems can include persistent bleeding, new cyclical pain or blood trapped behind scarring. Some people need further medication or surgery, including hysterectomy. Scarring may make later assessment of the lining more difficult. New symptoms should therefore be investigated rather than dismissed because the lining was previously treated; ablation does not remove the need for future gynaecological care.

Symptoms that need prompt or emergency assessment

Contact the treating team promptly for fever or chills, foul-smelling discharge, worsening abdominal pain, difficulty passing urine or bleeding heavier than expected. Persistent vomiting, urinary burning or symptoms that are not improving also need advice. Severe pain, heavy bleeding with faintness, breathing difficulty or becoming very unwell warrants emergency assessment.

If pregnancy is possible, take a test and contact a clinician promptly; a positive result requires early specialist assessment. Do not wait for a missed period, because bleeding may already have stopped after ablation. Sudden severe abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain, marked dizziness or collapse can signal an ectopic pregnancy or another emergency, even before a positive test.

Review the result over time

The effect on menstrual bleeding is assessed over the following months. Periods may become lighter, stop, or remain troublesome enough to need another approach. Ask when follow-up is due and what to do if bleeding or pain returns later. A good early result does not guarantee that no further treatment will ever be needed.

Return gradually to work, exercise and household tasks according to your recovery and the advice given. Some people feel ready within days; others need longer. Continue the agreed contraception and routine cervical screening, and report new bleeding even years later. Keep a record of the ablation method and date so future clinicians know about the changes to the uterine cavity.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ablation is intended for selected people with heavy menstrual bleeding who do not want a future pregnancy. Evaluation of the lining and uterine cavity comes before device selection.

Contraception remains necessary after treatment. A pregnancy test and early assessment are important when pregnancy is possible, even when periods have stopped.

How BeMama can help

Prepare questions about the treatment goal, alternatives, contraceptive plan and recovery support. BeMama can help organize that discussion, but cannot determine whether ablation or fertility treatment is suitable.

When to seek help

Seek prompt care for a suspected pregnancy after ablation. Severe abdominal pain, fainting, heavy bleeding, fever or marked illness after treatment needs urgent assessment.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Ablation reduces bleeding but does not sterilise you.
  • Do not choose it if you want to carry a future pregnancy.
  • Egg freezing and ovarian-reserve tests cannot make a scarred uterus safe for pregnancy.
  • The six methods differ in suitability, anaesthesia and availability.
  • Keep contraception, follow-up and warning signs in the recovery plan.

Frequently asked questions

Can pregnancy happen after endometrial ablation?

Yes. Ablation does not reliably prevent pregnancy, and a pregnancy afterwards can have serious complications. Continue the contraception plan agreed with your clinician.

Can I choose ablation if I want to carry a baby later?

It is not appropriate for that goal. Discuss alternatives for heavy bleeding before making a decision that damages the uterine lining.

Does regrowth of the lining make pregnancy safe again?

No. Residual or regrown lining does not reverse the risks created by ablation and scarring.

Can I stop contraception if my periods disappear?

No. Absent bleeding after ablation does not prove that ovulation has stopped or that menopause has occurred.

Do AMH and FSH tests prove that my eggs are good quality?

No. They help assess ovarian reserve and treatment planning, not directly measure egg quality or guarantee a baby.

Will freezing eggs allow me to carry a pregnancy safely afterwards?

Freezing eggs does not repair the uterine lining. Discuss realistic fertility-preservation and family-building options with a specialist before ablation.

Does every method require general anaesthesia and an eight-hour fast?

No. The method and your health determine the anaesthetic and preparation. Follow the exact fasting and medication instructions from your team.

Are all six techniques available at every clinic?

No. Devices and expertise vary. The team must also check whether a method suits the size, shape and condition of your uterus.

Is watery blood-stained discharge always an infection?

No. It can occur during normal recovery. Foul smell, fever, increasing pain or heavy bleeding needs medical advice rather than simple reassurance.

What should I do about a positive pregnancy test after ablation?

Contact a clinician promptly for early specialist assessment. Severe pain, shoulder-tip pain, faintness or heavy bleeding needs urgent or emergency care; do not wait for a routine appointment.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
